---
name: practices-verification
description: "Use when checking whether a declared behavior works on its intended target, challenging whether proposed proof can establish it, or building or maintaining an assigned verification driver. Not for delivery acceptance, general code review, root-cause investigation or product repairs."
---

# Practices: Verification

Verification turns an adopted expected outcome into an observation, made on the target the claim is about, that can tell the outcome apart from a specific wrong behavior. Start from what could still be wrong while the checks are green. A mock may have answered in place of the real interaction, the run may have hit another build, the probe may have seen only an acknowledgement, or the fixture may never have reached the case. Choose the cheapest observation that would catch that, make it or reuse one that already did, and report exactly what the evidence establishes.

You work under your current assignment and its actual permissions. Loading this practice grants no writes, commands or target access, and it leaves the expected outcome, the product code, the product tests and acceptance with their current owners. A wrong or unsettled expectation goes back to whoever owns it. An unexplained failure goes back to your caller with its evidence, and the caller decides who diagnoses it.

Project specifics live in the project's own verification skill under `.agents/skills/verify-<app>/`. Creating or maintaining that skill is the work of `practices-verification-maintenance`. When your current task is an observation, including the live pass that practice runs on a skill it just wrote or updated, continue the observation here. Hand off to `practices-verification-maintenance` only when your own task is creating or maintaining the project skill and the request authorizes that work. During an observation, report a missing or stale skill as a setup gap and name that practice as the route.

Make the observations yourself. IF your grant allows helpers and an exact collection is worth delegating, load `practices-manage-agents` and return the bounded commission; open the evidence each helper brings back and judge yourself whether it supports the claim.

## Workflow

1. **Establish the claim and the expected outcome.** Read the governing expectation, such as the spec, the plan obligation, the issue or the contract, and write the claim the way the user or caller would see it. Name one concrete wrong behavior the check must catch and one materially different allowed behavior it must accept. Take the expected result from that governing source, never from the implementation or from what the app does today. Work inside the caller's scope, gates and authority. When meaning is missing or two sources disagree, return the exact question to the caller instead of inventing an oracle. For example, the adopted ordering is per pane and an existing assertion demands global order, so it rejects valid implementations. Keep the allowed behavior and return the oracle problem to whoever owns the expectation; two agents agreeing on a new expected outcome to get green is never the fix. Completion: the claim, its source, the wrong behavior and the allowed alternative are written down, or the exact question is returned.

2. **Find the project's details, then choose the observation route.** MUST load `references/project-verification-selection.md` and return the selected project verification skill with the detail this claim needs, or its absent or conflicting result. Apply a selected skill's app-specific instructions to this claim; they add mechanics and never add permissions. With an absent result, keep the setup gap and make only the bounded check your grant permits with the method in this skill; an observation request never writes a project skill or starts `practices-verification-maintenance`. Then read the project's established commands, drivers and harnesses, trace the entry point to the effect the claim names, and choose an observation that rejects the wrong behavior and accepts the allowed alternative, at the cheapest boundary where the wrong behavior stays real ([a check counts only if the wrong behavior could make it fail where it runs](../principle-write-tests-that-can-fail/SKILL.md)). A pure domain rule proven by an honest focused test needs no app launch. A skill-only or schema-only assignment uses structural evidence, names the behavior it leaves unevaluated and runs no unrelated app. When the claim is comparative or quantitative (faster, smaller, fewer errors) or scores a prompt, classifier or skill, set the workload, the baseline or comparator, the repetitions and the deciding result before the run, add a negative control where you can, and scale the rigor to the noise and the stakes ([set the baseline and the deciding result before you look](../principle-experiment-before-proposing/SKILL.md)). Before a build exists, judge whether the route can reach the outcome at all and what it still needs, and describe no future observation as if it ran. Completion: the route names what stays real, the target it runs against and why a cheaper route would miss the wrong behavior, or the feasibility answer names what the route still needs.

3. **Check the target and whether existing evidence applies.** Name the actual app, binary or package, its build or source where that matters, and its configuration, client, state or fixtures and entry point. Before you reuse a test run or an earlier observation, compare what it depended on with this target, and reuse it where they still match ([evidence holds only for the version, target and dependencies it observed](../principle-verify-before-accepting/SKILL.md)). Equal source doesn't show that the installed target matches. A source change unrelated to the claim doesn't invalidate an observation. When a current real integration test already drives the exact interaction and its rejection case, reuse it and add no manual journey just so the check looks independent. Run again for a changed dependency, a specific doubt or a gate that requires it. Completion: the target and its dependencies are named, and each piece of evidence you will rely on is marked reused, with the dependencies that still match, or needing a run.

4. **Prepare and observe within the grant.** When a run is needed, find the signal that says the target is ready for use, which an answering port or a live process doesn't give, and isolate the state or instance the run uses. Once that signal shows the target is ready, drive the action the claim names and look at its consequence where the user or caller would see it, including any failure, round trip, restart or overlap the claim covers ([proof is the feature working through its real entry, seen where the user would see it](../principle-prove-it-works/SKILL.md)). Wait on a bounded completion signal that the operation owns. An acknowledgement, an idle prompt or a healthy process is not the outcome; a save that shows a success toast and loses the body on reopen fails a persistence claim, so check persistence by reopening or reading back. Load the depth for the surface the route crosses:
   - IF the claim requires browser behavior, load `references/browser-observation.md` and return the checked browser route and its observations, or the exact outcome you couldn't reach.
   - IF the claim requires native app behavior, load `references/native-observation.md` and return the native target and its behavior evidence, including what building or launching alone didn't establish.
   - IF the claim requires a CLI or TUI, load `references/terminal-observation.md` and return the correlated terminal action and result, with the cleanup you owned.
   - IF the claim concerns a service, a protocol or a library's caller, load `references/service-and-library-observation.md` and return the response and the state or effect evidence, or the interaction that stays unobserved.
   - IF an absent or broken route prevents the observation and the assignment explicitly includes verification-driver work and names its paths, load `references/verification-drivers.md` and return the driver changes and the observation they made, or the exact scope, seam or prerequisite gap. Write access to product code or product tests is not that assignment.

   Completion: the action you drove, the target it ran against and the result you saw are recorded, or the point where the run stopped is named.

5. **Challenge the observation.** Ask whether this check could pass on the wrong target, through an inert probe, with a fixture that never reached the case or with the interaction replaced, and whether it could reject behavior the contract allows. Where the answer is uncertain and your grant allows it, decide with a known-good and a known-bad case, an independent readback or another deciding check. A driver that exits 0 while its probe can't see a known failure can't decide the claim, and its exit 0 is not a pass. A sensitivity check you couldn't make stays a named gap. Don't change product code or cause a fault only because sensitivity would be useful. When a deliberate break made after the fix is caught, report it as sensitivity in the order the runs happened, never as a red seen before the fix or as tests written first. Completion: each observation you rely on names the wrong behavior it can catch and how you know, or names its missing sensitivity as a gap.

6. **Keep the evidence and place the gap.** Keep the action and result evidence and the command output where the project or the assignment already keeps them. Clean only the residue your run created, after the evidence is safe. When the evidence supports it, name the kind of gap: an unreachable target or setup, a driver defect, product behavior that contradicts the adopted outcome, a disputed expectation or stale project instructions. When a prerequisite such as a seed is unavailable, report the readiness gap and keep the outcome and its hard case; deleting the case to get a result is never allowed. When the cause is unknown, return the observed failure and the missing evidence that would decide it, without guessing a kind or starting a repair. Repair only what your assignment owns, such as a named driver path. A product defect found during a verification-only assignment goes with its evidence to whoever owns the implementation, even when you are asked to fix it while checking. Completion: the evidence location is stated and the evidence survives cleanup, and each gap has its kind or is returned as unknown with the evidence that would decide it.

7. **Report what the evidence supports.** Say what you ran or reused, the target and path it covered, what you observed and what stays unverified. For each claim, say whether the evidence supports it at the build and target the claim is about, and narrow the claim to what was shown ([name what the evidence doesn't cover instead of rounding up](../principle-verify-before-accepting/SKILL.md)). No checks discovered or run is not green. A missing observation is unknown, which is different from zero failures, and an inconclusive run is not a pass. A feasibility answer says whether the route is viable and what it still needs, and claims nothing about the feature. When adequate proof already closes the claim, stop instead of inventing another check. Completion: each claim is marked supported, unsupported or unknown with the evidence it rests on, and every unverified interaction and setup gap is listed.

## Return

Return to your caller the claim and its expected-outcome source, the project verification skill you used or the setup gap, the route and the target, each observation you ran or reused with where its evidence lives, the conclusion each claim supports and the gaps by kind, with any unknown cause returned alongside the evidence that would decide it.

## Completion

Not done while the observed target is unnamed, you haven't said whether a run happened, an observation you rely on names no wrong behavior it can catch, an unverified interaction or setup gap is missing from the report, or an unknown failure was given a cause or repaired instead of returned.
